main.title: Solstice
main.subtitle: Software Creations · Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Solstice is Software Creations' isometric puzzle adventure for the NES. The wizard Shadax enters the fortress of Kâstleröck to collect six pieces of the Staff of Demnos and rescue Princess Eleanor from Morbius. Its 250 rooms form a connected space, with each chamber presenting another arrangement of platforms, objects and hazards. Shadax can jump, lift and place objects. Those few actions make an apparently compact room demanding, because reaching a doorway can depend on understanding how several objects occupy the same three-dimensional space.

cards.heading: A fortress built from puzzles
cards.text: Solstice is Software Creations' isometric puzzle adventure for the NES. The wizard Shadax enters the fortress of Kâstleröck to collect six pieces of the Staff of Demnos and rescue Princess Eleanor from Morbius. Its 250 rooms form a connected space, with each chamber presenting another arrangement of platforms, objects and hazards. Shadax can jump, lift and place objects. Those few actions make an apparently compact room demanding, because reaching a doorway can depend on understanding how several objects occupy the same three-dimensional space.

cards.heading: A potion changes the room
cards.text: Four kinds of potion can grant temporary protection, remove moving objects, stop time or reveal invisible objects. Their effects last within the current room, encouraging the player to use a limited supply where it creates a practical opening. A falling block frozen in place can become a step. Other blocks can be moved into routes over dangerous floors. The isometric view makes these arrangements immediately visible, while judging their heights and positions remains part of solving the problem.

cards.heading: Remember the way back
cards.text: A map records visited rooms and their possible exits, helping the player relate individual puzzles to the larger fortress. Keys, hidden passages and useful items make a familiar chamber worth returning to later. Software Creations had previously concentrated on conversions; Solstice was its first original game. Tim Follin's elaborate score gives the opening a striking musical presence before the careful movement begins. The later Super NES sequel, Equinox, continued this interest in spaces whose routes have to be assembled through objects and observation.

main.title: Super Star Soldier
main.subtitle: A shooter built around the high-score challenge
main.summary: On July 6, 1990 Hudson Soft released Super Star Soldier for the PC Engine in Japan.

cards.heading: A shooter built around the high-score challenge
cards.text: Hudson Soft released Super Star Soldier for the PC Engine in Japan on July 6, 1990. The vertical shooter continues the Star Soldier series through eight stages and several upgradeable weapons. Timed modes associated with Hudson's Caravan competitions let players compare scores from a short, fixed section of play.

cards.heading: Two and five minutes turn the level into a test
cards.text: Timed modes tied to the Caravan tradition isolate a short window of play and make scores comparable, encouraging memorization, calculated risk and optimized routes.

cards.heading: Flamethrowers, electricity and heat-seeking missiles
cards.text: The game includes a variety of weapons including flamethrowers, electricity, spread guns and heat-seeking missiles. It consists of eight levels.

cards.heading: Caravan culture brings the arcade into the living room
cards.text: Caravan tournaments and score-attack modes gave players a shared target even when practising on home consoles. Repeating a timed section allowed them to compare routes, take calculated risks and improve a score before a competition.

main.title: Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake
main.summary: Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake is a 1990 action-adventure stealth game developed and published by Konami for the MSX2.

cards.heading: Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake
cards.text: Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake is a 1990 action-adventure stealth game developed and published by Konami for the MSX2. The second mainline installment in the Metal Gear series, it serves as a sequel to the original Metal Gear (1987). Set in 1999, a few years after the events of the original game, Solid Snake must infiltrate a heavily defended territory in Central Asia known as Zanzibar Land to rescue a kidnapped scientist and destroy the revised "Metal Gear D". The game significantly evolved the stealth-based game system of its predecessor, and uses a storyline dealing with themes such as the nature of warfare and nuclear proliferation.

cards.heading: Kojima returns to Solid Snake
cards.text: Metal Gear 2 was written and designed by series's creator Hideo Kojima, who conceived the game in response to Snake's Revenge (1990), a separately produced sequel that was being developed at the time for the NES specifically for the North American and European markets. Metal Gear 2 was released in Japan to positive critical reception, and retrospective reviews have labeled it as one of the best 8-bit games ever made. It was followed by a sequel, Metal Gear Solid, and was released worldwide for the PlayStation in 1998. Metal Gear 2 was re-released alongside the original Metal Gear in the Subsistence version of Metal Gear Solid 3 (2006) with a full English translation and other revisions, which was used for further re-releases on the Metal Gear Solid HD Collection and the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection.

main.title: Devil's Crush
main.subtitle: Devil's Crush Turns Pinball into a Gothic Dungeon
main.summary: On July 20, 1990 Naxat Soft released Devil Crash for the PC Engine in Japan, later known in the West as Devil's Crush.

cards.heading: Devil's Crush Turns Pinball into a Gothic Dungeon
cards.text: Naxat Soft released Devil Crash for the PC Engine in Japan on July 20, 1990, later known overseas as Devil's Crush. Compile's pinball game uses a vertically scrolling table filled with demons, symbols and hidden bonus rooms. Players build scores by hitting targets, opening routes and keeping the ball moving between its sections.

cards.heading: A scrolling table three screens high
cards.text: The playfield of Devil's Crush consists of a free scrolling pinball table three screens high. There are three pairs of flippers.

cards.heading: Targets feel like inhabitants of the table
cards.text: Faces, demons and other creatures react when struck by the ball. Their movement gives individual targets recognisable appearances while indicating successful hits. The Gothic figures fill the same table through which the player must keep the ball in play.

cards.heading: Nudging the table, risking a tilt and finding bonus rooms
cards.text: The player can nudge/bump the table to influence the ball's path. Using the tilt button too much will result in the game "tilting" and the flippers will stop working, causing a lost ball. There are many targets to shoot for and hidden bonus rooms.

main.title: Dr. Mario
main.subtitle: Dr. Mario Turns Falling Pieces into a Visual Diagnosis
main.summary: On July 27, 1990 Nintendo takes Mario out of the platform game and places him beside a bottle full of viruses.

cards.heading: Dr. Mario Turns Falling Pieces into a Visual Diagnosis
cards.text: Nintendo released Dr. Mario on July 27, 1990. Its falling-capsule puzzle places Mario beside a bottle containing coloured viruses. Players arrange capsule halves into matching lines to remove those fixed targets. Each capsule carries two colours, so placing one half usefully can leave the other obstructing a later move.

cards.heading: Moving and rotating two-colour capsules
cards.text: Dr. Mario is a falling block tile-matching video game. Mario assumes the role of a doctor, tossing two-colored medical capsules into a medicine bottle representing the playing field. This area is populated by viruses of three colors – red, yellow, and blue – which stay in their starting positions until removed. In a style similar to Tetris, the player manipulates each capsule as it vertically falls, able to move it left or right and rotate it 90 degrees clockwise or counter-clockwise.

cards.heading: Four matching colours clear viruses and release falling pieces
cards.text: When matching colors of capsule halves and viruses touch sequentially 4-in-a-row, they disappear. Any remaining half or whole capsules which are not supported will fall to the bottom of the playing field or until hitting another supported object, and any new 4-in-a-row alignments also disappear. The main objective is to eliminate all viruses from the playing field, finishing each level.

cards.heading: Choosing the speed and sending capsules to an opponent
cards.text: The options screen configures the starting level, game speed, and music. The player chooses a starting level between 0 and 20 that determines the number of viruses to clear, and one of three speeds of the falling capsules. The player's score is based on the elimination of viruses and the chosen game speed, with bonus points for clearing more than 1 in a single line. Dr. Mario offers a multiplayer gaming mode in which two players compete in separate playing fields. Each player's goal is to clear the private playing field of viruses first. Eliminating multiple viruses or initiating chain reactions can add capsules to the opponent's playing field. A player wins a single game upon eliminating all the viruses or upon the other player's bottle filling. The first player to win three games wins overall.

main.title: Shadow of the Ninja
main.subtitle: Shadow of the Ninja Turns Co-op into an Eight-Bit Choreography
main.summary: On August 10, 1990 Natsume released Kage for Famicom in Japan, the game later known in the West as Shadow of the Ninja.

cards.heading: Shadow of the Ninja Turns Co-op into an Eight-Bit Choreography
cards.text: Natsume released Kage for the Famicom in Japan on August 10, 1990, later known overseas as Shadow of the Ninja. One or two players guide Hayate and Kaede through platforming stages filled with enemies and traps. Katana and chain weapons offer different attack ranges, while climbing and hanging below overhangs provide ways through its confined spaces.

cards.heading: Two ninjas, climbing and a costly thunderstorm attack
cards.text: Shadow of the Ninja is a side-scrolling platform game that can be played by up to two players simultaneously, with one player controlling Hayate (a ninja in purple) and the other as Kaede (a kunoichi in orange). In either mode, the player can decide which character they want to control before the game begins. There are no actual performance differences between either character. The player can run, crouch, climb ladders, attack, and jump like in most side-scrolling action games as well as hang onto an overhang and move under it. If the player has more than half of their vitality remaining, they can perform a special attack by holding a button for an extended period, summoning a thunderstorm that will damage all on-screen enemies, but at the cost of roughly half of their maximum vitality.

cards.heading: Katana, kusarigama and limited throwing weapons
cards.text: The katana works at close range, while the kusarigama reaches farther and can strike diagonally upward. Choosing between them changes where the player wants to stand. Collecting a duplicate weapon raises its power, but taking too much damage can remove that improvement. Shuriken and grenades provide temporary ranged attacks until their supply runs out. Item boxes also hold vitality potions, giving exploration a practical purpose. Hidden upgrades can eventually let a player carry both main weapons and switch the answer to suit the next enemy.

cards.heading: Five levels and a shared supply of continues
cards.text: Shadow of the Ninja consists of five levels with fourteen stages, with the first four levels being divided into three stages and the final level into two. The player fights numerous types of enemy characters throughout each level, including bosses and sub-bosses. Once a boss has been defeated it will explode, this explosion will heal players the closer they are to it, since actually the same amount of health from one level will be carried to the next one until either recovered with potions or by dying. The game ends if the player loses all of their vitality and only five chances are provided to continue. If two players are playing the game, their continues will be shared.

main.title: Little Nemo: The Dream Master
main.subtitle: A journey through sleep
main.summary: Little Nemo: The Dream Master is Capcom’s NES platform adventure based on the animated film and, behind it, Winsor McCay’s comic-strip dreamer. Nemo travels through colourful dream worlds on a journey to rescue the king of Slumberland from the Nightmare King. His own abilities are limited, but friendly creatures can provide other ways to move. The stages give those borrowed abilities a purpose: finding the keys needed to open an exit often requires exploring above, below and beyond the most obvious route through a scene.

cards.heading: A journey through sleep
cards.text: Little Nemo: The Dream Master is Capcom’s NES platform adventure based on the animated film and, behind it, Winsor McCay’s comic-strip dreamer. Nemo travels through colourful dream worlds on a journey to rescue the king of Slumberland from the Nightmare King. His own abilities are limited, but friendly creatures can provide other ways to move. The stages give those borrowed abilities a purpose: finding the keys needed to open an exit often requires exploring above, below and beyond the most obvious route through a scene.

cards.heading: Candy buys a different ability
cards.text: Feeding candy to particular animals lets Nemo ride them or use their powers. A frog, gorilla or mole changes which parts of a level can be reached and how obstacles can be approached. Choosing a creature therefore amounts to choosing a method of exploration. The same wall or gap may become manageable with the appropriate helper. These changes give the dream setting a practical logic: strange encounters offer new movements, and the player learns to connect the appearance of an animal with a possible route.

cards.heading: Keys beyond the obvious path
cards.text: The exit’s locks make collecting keys essential, but the required total becomes clear only when Nemo reaches the door. A stage can therefore demand a return to places passed earlier, using an animal’s ability to investigate more thoroughly. The levels extend in several directions rather than simply presenting a straight run to the right. That structure supports the dreamlike variety of their scenery while keeping a concrete objective in view. Each new landscape asks the player to learn how its creatures and passages fit together.

main.title: Wing Commander
main.summary: Wing Commander is the first game in Chris Roberts' space flight simulation Wing Commander franchise by Origin Systems.

cards.heading: Wing Commander
cards.text: Wing Commander is the first game in Chris Roberts' space flight simulation Wing Commander franchise by Origin Systems. The game was first released for MS-DOS on September 26, 1990, and was later ported to the Amiga, CD32 (256-color), Sega CD and the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, and re-released for the PC as Wing Commander I in 1994. An enhanced remake Super Wing Commander was made for the 3DO in 1994, and later ported to the Macintosh.

cards.heading: Wing Commander
cards.text: Two expansion packs for the game were released: Wing Commander: The Secret Missions in November 1990 and Wing Commander: The Secret Missions 2: Crusade in March 1991.

cards.heading: Wing Commander
cards.text: The game was considered a major step forward for space dogfight games, featuring graphics, audio, and a story campaign that invited comparison to the Star Wars films.  Set in the year 2654 and characterized by Chris Roberts as "World War II in space", it features a multinational cast of pilots from the "Terran Confederation" flying missions against the predatory, aggressive Kilrathi, a feline warrior race (heavily inspired by the Kzinti of Larry Niven's Known Space universe).

main.title: Gun-Nac
main.subtitle: A strange fleet overhead
main.summary: Gun-Nac is Compile’s vertically scrolling NES shooter, set in an artificial planetary system where a mysterious force has brought ordinary objects to hostile life. The premise allows an eccentric procession of enemies across eight stages. Beneath that playful appearance sits a generous weapon system: five primary guns, four kinds of bomb and several levels of upgrades. The player continually chooses what to collect and what to keep, making the strength and shape of the ship’s attack a central part of surviving the next wave.

cards.heading: A strange fleet overhead
cards.text: Gun-Nac is Compile’s vertically scrolling NES shooter, set in an artificial planetary system where a mysterious force has brought ordinary objects to hostile life. The premise allows an eccentric procession of enemies across eight stages. Beneath that playful appearance sits a generous weapon system: five primary guns, four kinds of bomb and several levels of upgrades. The player continually chooses what to collect and what to keep, making the strength and shape of the ship’s attack a central part of surviving the next wave.

cards.heading: Build the weapon you want
cards.text: Numbered pickups select the main gun, with options including a straightforward shot, a flamethrower and a guided boomerang. Primary fire has unlimited ammunition, while lettered pickups supply a separate stock of bombs. Repeatedly collecting the same type improves its level, so chasing every visible icon can be less useful than preserving a preferred weapon. Bomb upgrades also increase ammunition consumption. The system creates a small decision inside the scrolling action: whether a pickup will strengthen the current plan or replace it with something less suitable.

cards.heading: A shop between the storms
cards.text: Money collected during stages can be spent on upgrades in the shops between them. A wing pickup enlarges the ship and allows it to survive an additional hit, while also supporting stronger weapon upgrades. Those systems give a successful stretch of shooting consequences beyond the score display: surviving and collecting well helps prepare the next departure. Gun-Nac keeps that preparation within a brisk arcade rhythm, balancing the pleasure of increasingly powerful attacks with the need to read enemy movement and protect the ship carrying them.

main.title: Super Nintendo Entertainment System
main.subtitle: Super Famicom and the Super Nintendo family
main.summary: On November 21, 1990, Nintendo brings the Super Famicom to Japanese stores, successor to the Family Computer and the platform that would be known in the West as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.heading: Super Famicom Expands the Console's Vocabulary
cards.text: Nintendo launched the Super Famicom in Japan on November 21, 1990, succeeding the Family Computer. Known overseas as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, it expanded colour, background effects and sound capabilities. Its controller added four face buttons and two shoulder buttons. Launch games Super Mario World and F-Zero demonstrated different uses of the new hardware.

cards.heading: Two Shoulder Buttons Change the Grammar of the Hands
cards.text: The controller retains a directional pad while arranging four face buttons in a diamond. L and R shoulder buttons place two more commands under the index fingers. Games can assign these controls to running, attacks, rotation or selection without relying entirely on combinations. The layout gives developers more immediately accessible actions while preserving a familiar pad.

cards.heading: Super Mario World Teaches the New Machine Through Play
cards.text: Super Mario World arrived at the Japanese launch. Its map connects courses through secret exits and alternative routes, while Yoshi adds new abilities and interactions with enemies. More colours, sprites and animated backgrounds support these varied situations. The familiar platforming also gives players a practical way to explore what the new machine can display.

cards.heading: Depth Is Created by Moving the Plane
cards.text: Launch title F-Zero creates its circuit by rotating and scaling a large graphical plane using Mode 7. The effect produces depth and speed without a polygonal track. From an elevated viewpoint, players read broad curves and obstacles as the course moves beneath the vehicle. A particular background capability becomes the basis for the game's racing presentation.

cards.heading: More Powerful, but Still Built Around Sprites
cards.text: Sprites, multiple background layers, scaling and rotation effects support the Super Famicom's two-dimensional imagery. A broader palette and sample-based sound expand its presentation. Polygonal objects require a different solution: Nintendo's developers turned to additional hardware such as the Super FX chip. The library grew through both the console's built-in features and selected cartridge enhancements.

cards.heading: The PAL design arrives in Europe
cards.text: For European players, the Super Nintendo arrived in 1992. The PAL machine kept the rounded outline and multicolour controller buttons associated with the Japanese Super Famicom, rather than the angular purple-button design sold in North America.

cards.heading: The controller and its games
cards.text: The controller expanded the familiar directional pad and face buttons with shoulder buttons under the player's index fingers. Stereo sound and richer imagery gave designers more room, but the results were not confined to spectacle. Super Mario World offered a colourful landscape of secrets; A Link to the Past built an adventure around revisiting places with new abilities; Super Metroid made exploration feel lonely and uncertain.

cards.heading: A library of different experiences
cards.text: F-Zero and Super Mario Kart turned the new machine towards a different sensation: speed and competition. Looking across this library, the generational change becomes visible through contrasts. A single cartridge system could hold races, long journeys and quiet discoveries, each asking something different of the same controller.
